Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a condition that affects adults over the age of 50, causing pain and stiffness in the neck, shoulder, and hip areas. While there is no definitive way to predict when PMR will develop, research suggests that certain factors may increase the risk of developing the disease.

One study found that patients who took higher doses of prednisolone (a steroid medication) had a greater risk of experiencing prolonged symptoms and needing long-term steroid therapy. Additionally, certain genetic markers, such as HLA alleles, may also play a role in increasing the risk of late Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), which can be a complication of PMR.

Another study found that female patients with PMR were at increased risk for developing RA later in life. These findings suggest that sex and genetic factors may contribute to the development of both conditions.

While there is currently no guarantee that you will develop PMR, taking steps to manage your overall health, including maintaining a healthy weight, exercising regularly, and managing stress levels, can help reduce the risk of developing the condition. If you are experiencing symptoms of PMR, it is essential to consult with your doctor to discuss the best course of treatment.

In terms of predicting progression of valvar aortic stenosis (VAS), current research suggests that a more accurate prediction of disease progression can be made using non-invasive imaging techniques, such as STIR (Short Tau Inversion Recovery) MRI. This method can help identify calcification and other structural changes in the valve that may indicate impending stenosis.

It is essential to note that further studies are needed to confirm these findings and to determine the optimal timing for initiating valvar surgery. However, with ongoing research and advancements in diagnostic techniques, it is possible that more effective methods of predicting disease progression will be developed in the future.
